claim: Nociceptive information is relayed through the spinal cord dorsal horn, a critical area in sensory processing.
source: Nociceptive information is relayed through the spinal cord dorsal horn, a critical area in sensory processing.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Photoactivation of CR interneurons in vivo resulted in a significant nocifensive behavior that was morphine sensitive.
source: Photoactivation of CR interneurons in vivo resulted in a significant nocifensive behavior that was morphine sensitive, caused a conditioned place aversion, and was enhanced by spared nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing morphine dose-dependent reduction in photostimulation-induced nocifensive behavior (Figure 8A).

claim: Photoactivation of CR interneurons in vivo caused a conditioned place aversion.
source: Photoactivation of CR interneurons in vivo resulted in a significant nocifensive behavior that was morphine sensitive, caused a conditioned place aversion, and was enhanced by spared nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing conditioned place aversion testing results (Figure 8C-D).

claim: Photoactivation of CR interneurons in vivo was enhanced by spared nerve injury.
source: Photoactivation of CR interneurons in vivo resulted in a significant nocifensive behavior that was morphine sensitive, caused a conditioned place aversion, and was enhanced by spared nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased photostimulation response duration following SNI surgery (Figure 8E-H).

claim: Halorhodopsin-mediated inhibition of CR interneurons elevated sensory thresholds.
source: Furthermore, halorhodopsin-mediated inhibition of these interneurons elevated sensory thresholds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds during photoinhibition (Figure 8B).

claim: Dorsal horn circuits that involve excitatory CR neurons are important for the generation and amplification of pain.
source: Our results suggest that dorsal horn circuits that involve excitatory CR neurons are important for the generation and amplification of pain and identify these interneurons as a future analgesic target.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CR interneurons represent a future analgesic target.
source: Our results suggest that dorsal horn circuits that involve excitatory CR neurons are important for the generation and amplification of pain and identify these interneurons as a future analgesic target.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: Alterations to neuronal circuits within the dorsal horn can directly contribute to neuropathic and inflammatory pain.
source: It is well established that alterations to neuronal circuits within the dorsal horn can directly contribute to neuropathic and inflammatory pain, as well as persistent itch (Basbaum et al., 2009; Braz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alterations to neuronal circuits within the dorsal horn can directly contribute to persistent itch.
source: It is well established that alterations to neuronal circuits within the dorsal horn can directly contribute to neuropathic and inflammatory pain, as well as persistent itch (Basbaum et al., 2009; Braz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Understanding of the neuronal circuits associated with particular sensory modalities in the dorsal horn remains limited.
source: Despite this being a region of immense biological importance, our understanding of the neuronal circuits associated with particular sensory modalities remains limited (Todd, 2010; Peirs and Seal, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Several groups have recently implicated neurochemically-distinct subpopulations of dorsal horn interneurons with the perception of both acute and chronic pain states.
source: To address this knowledge gap, several groups have recently implicated neurochemically-distinct subpopulations of dorsal horn interneurons with the perception of both acute and chronic pain states (Duan et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015; Peirs et al., 2015; Petitjean et al., 2015; Boyle et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Much of the research effort on spinal circuits has focused on inhibition.
source: Historically, much of the research effort on spinal circuits has focused on inhibition (Zeilhofer et al., 2012), and a growing number of discrete inhibitory interneuron populations have now been identified as substrates for sensory gating in the spinal cord (Duan et al., 2014; Petitjean et al., 2015; Foster et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2016; Boyle et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A growing number of discrete inhibitory interneuron populations have been identified as substrates for sensory gating in the spinal cord.
source: Historically, much of the research effort on spinal circuits has focused on inhibition (Zeilhofer et al., 2012), and a growing number of discrete inhibitory interneuron populations have now been identified as substrates for sensory gating in the spinal cord (Duan et al., 2014; Petitjean et al., 2015; Foster et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2016; Boyle et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Understanding of the role excitatory interneurons play in sensory processing is far less developed than for inhibitory interneurons.
source: In contrast, our understanding of the role excitatory interneurons play in sensory processing is far less developed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the state of the field as described in the manuscript.

claim: Excitatory interneurons are considered to provide polysynaptic relays linking circuits dedicated to innocuous and noxious sensory input.
source: Generally, excitatory interneurons are considered to provide polysynaptic relays linking circuits dedicated to innocuous and noxious sensory input, with inhibitory populations normally modulating the passage of information through these pathways (Takazawa and MacDermott, 2010; Duan et al., 2014; Punnakkal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibitory populations normally modulate the passage of information through excitatory pathways in the dorsal horn.
source: Generally, excitatory interneurons are considered to provide polysynaptic relays linking circuits dedicated to innocuous and noxious sensory input, with inhibitory populations normally modulating the passage of information through these pathways (Takazawa and MacDermott, 2010; Duan et al., 2014; Punnakkal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The excitatory interneuron population is more than double that of inhibitory interneurons in laminae I and II.
source: Such a limited role for excitatory interneurons is surprising given this population is more than double that of inhibitory interneurons in the region (laminae I and II) (Polgár et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Approximately 85% of the synaptic connections in the dorsal horn are excitatory.
source: Furthermore, detailed paired recording studies have also shown that ~85% of the synaptic connections in the DH are excitatory (Santos et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most calretinin-expressing (CR) neurons in laminae I and II exhibit specific electrophysiological, morphological and neurochemical properties consistent with an excitatory phenotype.
source: Notably, we have recently shown that most calretinin-expressing (CR) neurons in laminae I and II exhibit specific electrophysiological, morphological and neurochemical properties consistent with an excitatory phenotype and respond to noxious peripheral stimulation (Smith et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Most calretinin-expressing (CR) neurons in laminae I and II respond to noxious peripheral stimulation.
source: Notably, we have recently shown that most calretinin-expressing (CR) neurons in laminae I and II exhibit specific electrophysiological, morphological and neurochemical properties consistent with an excitatory phenotype and respond to noxious peripheral stimulation (Smith et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of CR neurons causes nocifensive behaviors.
source: In fact, chemogenetic activation of CR neurons has been shown to cause nocifensive behaviors and dorsal horn activation patterns consistent with mechanical hypersensitivity (Peirs et al., 2015), whereas genetic ablation of these neurons can cause a selective loss of light punctate touch sensation (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of CR neurons causes dorsal horn activation patterns consistent with mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: In fact, chemogenetic activation of CR neurons has been shown to cause nocifensive behaviors and dorsal horn activation patterns consistent with mechanical hypersensitivity (Peirs et al., 2015), whereas genetic ablation of these neurons can cause a selective loss of light punctate touch sensation (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetic ablation of CR neurons can cause a selective loss of light punctate touch sensation.
source: In fact, chemogenetic activation of CR neurons has been shown to cause nocifensive behaviors and dorsal horn activation patterns consistent with mechanical hypersensitivity (Peirs et al., 2015), whereas genetic ablation of these neurons can cause a selective loss of light punctate touch sensation (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A specific excitatory interneuron population in the deep dorsal horn that transiently express VGLUT3 relays low threshold input to CR neurons.
source: Prior work has established that a specific excitatory interneuron population in the deep dorsal horn that transiently express VGLUT3 relays low threshold input to CR neurons (Peirs et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 78.3 ± 4% of CR-IR neurons express YFP in CRCre;Ai32 mice.
source: Analysis of immunolabelling patterns confirmed YFP expression was highly localized to the CR-IR population, with 78.3 ± 4% (SD) of CR-IR neurons expressing YFP (1454 cells counted in three animals), and 71.5% (±2%) of YFP-IR neurons expressing CR (1767 cells counted in three animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunolabelling analysis.

claim: 71.5% (±2%) of YFP-IR neurons express CR in CRCre;Ai32 mice.
source: Analysis of immunolabelling patterns confirmed YFP expression was highly localized to the CR-IR population, with 78.3 ± 4% (SD) of CR-IR neurons expressing YFP (1454 cells counted in three animals), and 71.5% (±2%) of YFP-IR neurons expressing CR (1767 cells counted in three animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunolabelling analysis.

claim: The spinal distribution of YFP expression in CRCre;Ai32 mice mirrors the distribution of immunoreactivity for CR.
source: The spinal distribution of YFP expression in these mice mirrored the distribution of immunoreactivity for CR (CR-IR), forming a plexus of cell bodies, dendrites and axons that was concentrated in lamina II (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: YFP expression in CRCre;Ai32 mice forms a plexus of cell bodies, dendrites and axons that is concentrated in lamina II.
source: The spinal distribution of YFP expression in these mice mirrored the distribution of immunoreactivity for CR (CR-IR), forming a plexus of cell bodies, dendrites and axons that was concentrated in lamina II (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A smaller population of cells that express CR transiently during their development are captured in the CRCre;Ai32 line.
source: These data validate spinal interneuron expression of YFP, and by extension ChR2 in the CRCre;Ai32 line, but also imply that a smaller population of cells that express CR transiently during their development, described previously (Peirs et al., 2015), are also captured.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete overlap between YFP and CR expression, with support from previous literature.

claim: Excitatory CR+ neurons exhibited the voltage gated potassium current Ia.
source: Excitatory CR+ neurons exhibited several characteristic electrophysiological features including the voltage gated potassium current Ia (upper left, protocol below), high frequency spontaneous excitatory drive (upper right), and delayed firing (DF) discharge in response to depolarizing current injection (lower left, current step protocol below).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Excitatory CR+ neurons exhibited high frequency spontaneous excitatory drive.
source: Excitatory CR+ neurons exhibited several characteristic electrophysiological features including the voltage gated potassium current Ia (upper left, protocol below), high frequency spontaneous excitatory drive (upper right), and delayed firing (DF) discharge in response to depolarizing current injection (lower left, current step protocol below).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Excitatory CR+ neurons exhibited delayed firing (DF) discharge in response to depolarizing current injection.
source: Excitatory CR+ neurons exhibited several characteristic electrophysiological features including the voltage gated potassium current Ia (upper left, protocol below), high frequency spontaneous excitatory drive (upper right), and delayed firing (DF) discharge in response to depolarizing current injection (lower left, current step protocol below).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Photostimulation evoked robust inward photocurrents in YFP neurons in the CRCre;Ai32 line.
source: Consistent with our previous work, patch clamp recordings from YFP neurons in the CRCre;Ai32 line yielded characteristic electrophysiological features indicative of excitatory interneurons (Figure 1B). In voltage clamp, these cells exhibited robust inward photocurrents in response to photostimulation (n = 29 cells from 16 animals), which increased with stimulation intensity (0.01–16 mW, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Photocurrents in YFP neurons increased with stimulation intensity (0.01–16 mW).
source: In voltage clamp, these cells exhibited robust inward photocurrents in response to photostimulation (n = 29 cells from 16 animals), which increased with stimulation intensity (0.01–16 mW, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: YFP neurons in CRCre;Ai32 mice could reliably follow repetitive stimulation trains up to 10 Hz.
source: In current clamp, photostimulation evoked AP discharge, and these neurons were able to reliably follow repetitive stimulation trains up to 10 Hz, however, reliability decreased at higher frequencies (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Reliability of AP discharge in YFP neurons decreased at stimulation frequencies higher than 10 Hz.
source: In current clamp, photostimulation evoked AP discharge, and these neurons were able to reliably follow repetitive stimulation trains up to 10 Hz, however, reliability decreased at higher frequencies (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The latency between photostimulation onset and AP discharge in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons was 3.29 ± 0.21 ms.
source: The latency between photostimulation onset and AP discharge (i.e. recruitment delay) across this sample was 3.29 ± 0.21 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology recordings.

claim: A subset of CR neurons identified as inhibitory interneurons expressed YFP in CRCre;Ai32 mice.
source: We also assessed whether the subset of CR neurons identified in our previous work as inhibitory interneurons (Atypical CR neurons) expressed YFP (n = 13 cells from nine animals). Consistent with these earlier findings, a population of YFP expressing cells exhibited morphological and electrophysiologial features characteristic of an inhibitory phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Photostimulation in inhibitory YFP expressing neurons evoked larger inward photocurrents than observed in the excitatory population (459.72 ± 34.85 pA vs. 233.66 ± 56.16 pA).
source: Photostimulation in this subset of YFP expressing neurons evoked larger inward photocurrents than observed in the excitatory population (459.72 ± 34.85 pA vs. 233.66 ± 56.16 pA), which similarly increased with light intensity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The inhibitory YFP population had a shorter recruitment time than excitatory YFP neurons (2.39 ± 0.21 ms vs. 3.29 ± 0.38 ms).
source: The inhibitory YFP population could also reliably follow repetitive photostimulation at rates up to 10 Hz, but had a shorter recruitment time than excitatory YFP neurons (2.39 ± 0.21 ms vs. 3.29 ± 0.38 ms, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The CRCre;Ai32 mouse provides optogenetic control of both excitatory and inhibitory CR lineages.
source: Together, these data indicate that this CRCre;Ai32 mouse provides optogenetic control of both excitatory and inhibitory CR lineages (hereafter termed CR-ChR2 neurons).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing both excitatory and inhibitory CR neurons express ChR2.

claim: Some limited expression of CR is present in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) of rat and mouse.
source: Previous work has also shown that some limited expression of CR is present in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) of rat and mouse (Ren et al., 1993; Zhang et al., 2014), suggesting this tissue should also be assessed in CRCre;Ai32 animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GFP-labelled DRG cell bodies in CRCre;Ai32 mice typically had large soma (mean diameter 24.5 ± 5.1 µm).
source: This analysis showed GFP-labelled DRG cell bodies were occasionally observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, left). These cells typically had large soma (mean diameter 24.5 ± 5.1 µm; n = 53 cells in 30 sections from four animals), and expressed NF200 but lacked immunolabelling for substance P.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: GFP-labelled DRG cell bodies in CRCre;Ai32 mice expressed NF200 but lacked immunolabelling for substance P.
source: These cells typically had large soma (mean diameter 24.5 ± 5.1 µm; n = 53 cells in 30 sections from four animals), and expressed NF200 but lacked immunolabelling for substance P.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Only 11 out of 815 afferent terminals counted expressed YFP-immunolabelling in CRCre;Ai32 mice.
source: Given this finding, YFP expression was also assessed in the central terminals of several neurochemically-defined primary afferent classes in spinal cord sections. Specifically immunolabelling for VGLUT1 (myelinated low threshold mechanoreceptors; ALTMRs), substance P and CGRP (peptidergic C-fibres), prostatic acid phosphatase (Pap; non-peptidergic C-fibres), and VGLUT3 (C-fibre low threshold mechanoreceptors; CLTMRs) were assessed in tissue from CRCre;Ai32 animals (n = 2). Only 11 out of 815 afferent terminals counted expressed YFP-immunolabelling (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Virtually no co-expression of CR-IR was found in YFP boutons in laminae I-III (1 out of 397) in Advillin-eGFP mice.
source: To support this finding, spinal cord sections from an Advillin-eGFP mouse line (Avil-EGFP) were also analysed to further determine the extent of CR-expression in the central terminals of primary afferents (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F, n = 2 animals). We found virtually no co-expression of CR-IR in YFP boutons in laminae I-III (1 out of 397), and of YFP in CR-IR terminals (2/215).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F.

claim: Virtually no co-expression of YFP was found in CR-IR terminals in laminae I-III (2 out of 215) in Advillin-eGFP mice.
source: We found virtually no co-expression of CR-IR in YFP boutons in laminae I-III (1 out of 397), and of YFP in CR-IR terminals (2/215).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F.

claim: Occasional examples of CR and YFP co-expression were observed in terminals located in the deep medial lamina V in Advillin-eGFP mice.
source: In contrast, occasional examples of CR and YFP co-expression were observed in terminals located in the deep medial lamina V (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), but the incidence of these profiles was not formally analysed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Photostimulation of the spinal cord in in vitro and in vivo experiments selectively recruits central CR neurons and their processes.
source: Together, these data rule out the expression of ChR2 in the central terminals of primary afferents arborising in laminae I-III, and support the conclusion that photostimulation of the spinal cord in our in vitro and in vivo experiments selectively recruits central CR neurons and their processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing minimal ChR2 expression in primary afferents.

claim: Brief full-field photostimulation produced robust synaptic responses in CR-ChR2 neurons themselves.
source: Brief full-field photostimulation (16 mW, 1 ms) was applied to assess excitatory postsynaptic responses across various dorsal horn populations (n = 73 cells from 27 animals). Strikingly, robust synaptic responses were observed in the CR-ChR2 neurons themselves (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: oEPSCs were observed in 96.5% of CR-ChR2 recordings (28/29), indicating a high degree of interconnectivity in the CR-ChR2 population.
source: We observed oEPSCs in 96.5% of these recordings (28/29), indicating a high degree of interconnectivity in the CR-ChR2 population.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM recordings.

claim: The distribution of oEPSC latencies in CR-ChR2 neurons suggested they receive both a direct and delayed input following photostimulation (35% direct, 65% delayed).
source: The distribution of oEPSC latencies in CR-ChR2 neurons suggested they receive both a direct and delayed input following photostimulation (35% direct, 65% delayed, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Plexus recordings received mostly direct input (75% direct, 25% delayed).
source: Using the same defined window for direct and delayed input, plexus recordings received mostly direct input (75% direct, 25% delayed, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), whereas recordings dorsal to the YFP plexus exhibited a similar level of direct and delayed oEPSC input (57% direct, 43% delayed, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Recordings dorsal to the YFP plexus exhibited a similar level of direct and delayed oEPSC input (57% direct, 43% delayed).
source: Using the same defined window for direct and delayed input, plexus recordings received mostly direct input (75% direct, 25% delayed, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), whereas recordings dorsal to the YFP plexus exhibited a similar level of direct and delayed oEPSC input (57% direct, 43% delayed, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: oEPSC onset was significantly shorter for neurons within the YFP plexus compared to other populations (plexus = 4.75 ± 0.59 ms vs. YFP = 8.61 ± 1.23 ms, p=0.012; dorsal = 7.34 ± 1.06 ms, p=0.047).
source: Comparison of oEPSC characteristics identified a significantly shorter onset of the oEPSC response for neurons within the YFP plexus compared to other populations (Figure 2B, plexus = 4.75 ± 0.59 ms vs. YFP = 8.61 ± 1.23 ms, p=0.012; dorsal = 7.34 ± 1.06 ms, p=0.047).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Activation of CR-ChR2 neurons produces excitation that arrives first on nearby populations within the YFP plexus, before it reaches neurons dorsal to this region.
source: Thus, activation of CR-ChR2 neurons produces excitation that unsurprisingly arrives first on nearby populations within the YFP plexus, before it reaches neurons dorsal to this region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing shorter oEPSC latencies in plexus neurons.

claim: Interconnectivity of CR-ChR2 neurons indicates they form an excitatory network likely to enhance activity within the dorsal horn when recruited.
source: In addition, interconnectivity of CR-ChR2 neurons indicates they form an excitatory network likely to enhance activity within the dorsal horn when recruited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing high interconnectivity.

claim: Three response types were typically distinguished in current clamp recordings: subthreshold excitatory responses, suprathreshold excitatory responses, and inhibitory responses.
source: The impact of CR-ChR2 photostimulation on the activity of postsynaptic populations was also assessed in current clamp (Figure 2C, n = 22 cells, from 12 animals). Three response types were typically distinguished in these recordings; i) subthreshold excitatory responses, ii) suprathreshold excitatory responses (i.e. evoked AP discharge), and iii) inhibitory responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The incidence of each response type was similar among the YFP plexus and dorsal recordings.
source: The incidence of each response was similar among the YFP plexus and dorsal recordings (Figure 2D) including excitatory (56.3% and 66.6%) and inhibitory (37.5% and 25%) responses, with few neurons responding with AP discharge (6.2% and 8.4%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Optically evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (oIPSCs) were observed in all neuron populations studied (CR-ChR2 10/11, plexus 16/19, and dorsal neurons 4/7).
source: Optically evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (oIPSCs) were observed in all neuron populations studied (CR-ChR2 10/11, plexus 16/19, and dorsal neurons 4/7; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: oIPSC latency was similar among CR-ChR2, plexus, and dorsal recordings (CR-ChR2 = 7.9 ± 0.5 ms, plexus = 8.3 ± 0.6 ms, and dorsal = 5.7 ± 0.1 ms).
source: Comparison of oIPSC characteristics showed that oIPSC latency was similar among these recordings (CR-ChR2 = 7.9 ± 0.5 ms, plexus = 8.3 ± 0.6 ms, and dorsal = 5.7 ± 0.1 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM recordings.

claim: All neuron types exhibited responses consistent with direct and delayed oIPSC components.
source: All neuron types exhibited responses consistent with direct and delayed oIPSC components (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Delayed oIPSC components dominated in neurons within the YFP plexus (80.5% delayed vs. 19.5% direct).
source: Delayed oIPSCs components dominated in neurons within the YFP plexus (80.5% delayed vs. 19.5% direct), whereas a similar mix of direct and delayed oIPSC components were recorded in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons and neurons dorsal to the YFP plexus (excitatory CR-ChR2 = 53% delayed vs. 47% direct, and dorsal 59% delayed vs. 41% direct).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM recordings.

claim: A similar mix of direct and delayed oIPSC components were recorded in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons (53% delayed vs. 47% direct).
source: Delayed oIPSCs components dominated in neurons within the YFP plexus (80.5% delayed vs. 19.5% direct), whereas a similar mix of direct and delayed oIPSC components were recorded in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons and neurons dorsal to the YFP plexus (excitatory CR-ChR2 = 53% delayed vs. 47% direct, and dorsal 59% delayed vs. 41% direct).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM recordings.

claim: A similar mix of direct and delayed oIPSC components were recorded in neurons dorsal to the YFP plexus (59% delayed vs. 41% direct).
source: Delayed oIPSCs components dominated in neurons within the YFP plexus (80.5% delayed vs. 19.5% direct), whereas a similar mix of direct and delayed oIPSC components were recorded in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons and neurons dorsal to the YFP plexus (excitatory CR-ChR2 = 53% delayed vs. 47% direct, and dorsal 59% delayed vs. 41% direct).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM recordings.

claim: GABA-dominant responses were most common across all recordings (excitatory-CR-ChR2 = 72%, plexus = 65%, dorsal = 58%).
source: Across all recordings, GABA-dominant responses were most common (Figure 2F: excitatory- CR-ChR2 = 72%, plexus = 65%, dorsal = 58%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Glycine dominant responses were rare, and not observed at all in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons.
source: Glycine dominant responses were rare, and not observed at all in excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons, with remaining cells receiving mixed inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM recordings.

claim: Short latency direct inhibition likely comes through direct photostimulation of inhibitory CR-ChR2 neurons.
source: Short latency direct inhibition likely comes through direct photostimulation of inhibitory CR-ChR2 neurons, whereas polysynaptic pathways recruited by photostimulation of excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons are best placed to produce longer latency indirect inhibitory responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing both direct and indirect inhibitory responses.

claim: Polysynaptic pathways recruited by photostimulation of excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons are best placed to produce longer latency indirect inhibitory responses.
source: Short latency direct inhibition likely comes through direct photostimulation of inhibitory CR-ChR2 neurons, whereas polysynaptic pathways recruited by photostimulation of excitatory CR-ChR2 neurons are best placed to produce longer latency indirect inhibitory responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing both direct and indirect inhibitory responses.

claim: One third of the excitatory CR-ChR2 cells (4/12) exhibited increased post-stimulation sEPSC frequency.
source: A threshold of 4 standard deviations above the mean pre-stimulation sEPSC frequency was set to confidently identify recordings with increased post-photostimulation sEPSC frequency. Using this criterion one third of the excitatory CR-ChR2 cells (4/12) exhibited increased post-stimulation sEPSC frequency (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Post-stimulation sEPSC frequency did not increase in unidentified dorsal horn neurons (0/9).
source: In contrast, poststimulation sEPSC frequency did not increase in unidentified dorsal horn neurons (0/9), or inhibitory CR-ChR2 neurons (0/5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Post-stimulation sEPSC frequency did not increase in inhibitory CR-ChR2 neurons (0/5).
source: In contrast, poststimulation sEPSC frequency did not increase in unidentified dorsal horn neurons (0/9), or inhibitory CR-ChR2 neurons (0/5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology recordings.

claim: There was no correlation between the degree of potentiation and photocurrent amplitude (r2 = 0.00002).
source: Despite this, there was no correlation between the degree of potentiation and either photocurrent amplitude (Figure 3C left; r2 = 0.00002) or oEPSC amplitude (Figure 2C right; r2 = 0.056).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no correlation between the degree of potentiation and oEPSC amplitude (r2 = 0.056).
source: Despite this, there was no correlation between the degree of potentiation and either photocurrent amplitude (Figure 3C left; r2 = 0.00002) or oEPSC amplitude (Figure 2C right; r2 = 0.056).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Enhanced excitatory synaptic activity in CR-ChR2 neurons took ~20 s before returning to baseline.
source: Peristimulus histograms (Figure 3D) compared CR-ChR2 neuron responses that exhibited increased post-stimulation sEPSC frequency (n = 4) with CR-ChR2 neurons that exhibited similar baseline sEPSC frequency but no poststimulation increase (n = 5). This highlighted the dramatic and prolonged nature of enhanced excitatory synaptic activity in the post-stimulation period, taking ~20 s before returning to baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: These results are compatible with a model that features feedback excitation within the ChR2 network, capable of maintaining elevated excitatory signalling beyond the initial excitatory stimulus.
source: Together, these results are compatible with a model that features feedback excitation within the ChR2 network, capable of maintaining elevated excitatory signalling beyond the initial excitatory stimulus.
